"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
President Trump said today he's standing by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even in the
face of efforts to impeach him.
Trump spoke to reporters during an impromptu press briefing this afternoon, as NPR's Deepa
Shivaram reports.
Trump defended Hegseth, who is the target of an impeachment vote this week in Congress.
He said his Defense Secretary has succeeded in U.S. operations in Venezuela and Iran.
He certainly, I think, he's won the war on Iran, but he's certainly winning the war.
Iran would love to make a deal.
Trump's comments came during an unscheduled briefing with the press, where he brought
Dana White, the head of UFC, the ultimate fighting championship.
Trump posted on social media over the weekend jokingly offering White the job of being his
press secretary.
He asked White again during the briefing, but White declined and said he didn't want a role
in politics.
Deepa Shivaram, NPR News.
Congress is back to work in Washington today, the start of a six-week lame duck session,
as Republicans try to wrap up work before Democrats take control in January.
And today is also the new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller's, first day.
Shares of NVIDIA closed down more than 4 percent after the computer chipmaker, central
to the A.I. race, opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship
with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
She worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys chips from NVIDIA, and
Pierce John Ruich has more.
Pierce John Ruich.
A Tennessee judge is temporarily blocking the state from stopping certain immigrants
from legally driving.
Mariana Bacchiao of Member Station WPLN reports immigrant advocates are suing.
L.R., a nurse and DACA recipient in East Tennessee, has an hour-long commute to the rural hospital
where he works.
He has to be identified by his initials because he fears retaliation from immigration officials.
He says he hasn't been able to drive to work in recent weeks, despite having a valid
work permit.
"This left my coworkers in a bind as we are already experiencing a nursing shortage."
A coalition of immigrant advocates sued the state over the policy, which stems from a
sweeping immigration law that created a state agency to coordinate with federal authorities.
Governor Bill Lee says he's looking into the possibility of "unintended consequences"
of the law he championed.
For NPR News, I'm Mariana Bacchiao in Nashville.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Aerospace giant Boeing says it plans to cut 5 percent of its commercial airplane workforce
as the company struggles to increase its jetliner production rate.
Officials say the cuts will come through a mix of attrition and layoffs with notifications
starting next month.
Last month, Boeing said it missed production targets for its popular 737 models this year.
Boeing's targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month by the second half of next
year as it works to recover from a crisis of safety and quality that left the company
heavily in debt and under tighter scrutiny from regulators.
Musician Richard Lloyd has died at the age of 75.
He was a guitarist in the art/rock band Television.
And here's Isabella Gomez-Sarmiento has more.
Television grew out of the New York City punk scene in the 1970s, playing at clubs like
CBGB.
The interplay between the two guitarists, Richard Lloyd and Tom Berlaine, became a key
tenet of the band's improvisational approach to punk.
After releasing two albums, Television disbanded in 1978 and Lloyd went on to pursue solo projects.
But the band and Richard Lloyd's contributions to its kinetic sound are still cited as key
innovators in the development of alternative rock, influencing groups like REM, Pavement
and U2.
Isabella Gomez-Sarmiento, NPR News.
U.S. Futures contracts are trading in mixed territory at this hour.
Dow futures up about 105 points, NASDAQ futures down 18 points.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News in Washington.
